# Platform & Console knowledge brief

Platform & Console owns inference gateway policy, tenant configuration, safe rollouts, telemetry workflows, and the operator-facing console. The team uses LiteLLM for gateway work and Langfuse for observability and console workflows, reconciling code changes with product, security, and operational requirements.

# Platform & Console knowledge brief

Platform & Console owns inference gateway policy, tenant configuration, safe rollouts, telemetry workflows, and the operator-facing console. Team: Platform & Console

# Platform & Console knowledge brief

Platform & Console owns inference gateway policy, tenant configuration, safe rollouts, telemetry workflows, and the operator-facing console. The team uses LiteLLM for gateway work and Langfuse for observability and console workflows, reconciling code changes with product, security, and operational requirements.

## High-value source areas

These are retrieval hints, not access-control filters.

- codebases/litellm
- codebases/langfuse
- github/rbac-policy-bundle
- linear/engineering
- linear/design
- confluence/eng-platform
- confluence/product-docs
- slack/eng-platform
- slack/product

Lead: Priya Natarajan

## Representative sources in this corpus

# Platform & Console knowledge brief

Platform & Console owns inference gateway policy, tenant configuration, safe rollouts, telemetry workflows, and the operator-facing console. The team uses LiteLLM for gateway work and Langfuse for observability and console workflows, reconciling code changes with product, security, and operational requirements.

## High-value source areas

These are retrieval hints, not access-control filters.

- codebases/litellm
- codebases/langfuse
- github/rbac-policy-bundle
- linear/engineering
- linear/design
- confluence/eng-platform
- confluence/product-docs
- slack/eng-platform
- slack/product

Lead: Priya Natarajan

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Contributor Toolflow and Privileges Playbook\",\n  \"space\": \"company-handbook\",\n  \"author\": \"Asha Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"people-ops\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-10-02\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Evan Liu\",\n    \"Priya Kapoor\",\n    \"Marco Ruiz\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"onboarding\",\n    \"access-management\",\n    \"tooling\",\n    \"privileges\",\n    \"deprovisioning\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json\",\n    \"/confluence/company-handbook/02_roles-and-career/competency-maps-and-rotation-paths-2027.json\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"Overview\\n\\nPurpose: This playbook documents the standard tool access lifecycle for contributors at Redwood \\u2014 from first-day provisioning through promotions, cross-team rotations, and final deprovisioning. The emphasis is on fast enablement, least-privilege by default, auditable changes, and clear manager/engineer responsibilities.\\n\\nAudience: people-ops, hiring managers, engineering managers, IT, security reviewers, and new contributors.\\n\\nSummary of goals:\\n- Ensure 95% of new hires have usable accounts and core tool access within 8 business hours of start.\\n- Enforce least-privilege role assignments for 90% of contributors by role templates.\\n- Complete deprovisioning within 24 hours for offboarded contributors (per security SLA).\\n\\nKey principles\\n- Least privilege: grant only the roles required for the contributor\\u2019s current responsibilities.\\n- Role templates: use standardized permission packages (see Role \\u2192 Tool mapping).\\n- Manager-driven exceptions: any deviation requires manager justification and a 90-day review.\\n- Auditability: every access change must be recorded in Okta and the access-request ticket.\\n\\nRole \\u2192 Tool mapping (canonical templates)\\n| Role | GitHub | GCP (project) | Datadog | Jira | Slack | Console/Secrets | Notes |\\n|------|--------|----------------|---------|------|-------|----------------|-------|\\n| IC-Engineer-Level-1 | repo:read | viewer | dash:read | dev-project | full | vault:read | Standard new-hire dev access (no prod) |\\n| IC-Engineer-Level-2 | repo:write | dev-editor | dash:read | dev-squad | full | vault:read | Can merge to non-protected branches; needs sprint leads approval for protected branches |\\n| IC-Engineer-Level-3 | repo:admin* | staging-editor | dash:write | squad-admin | full | vault:deploy | Elevated staging access; production access by exception and 90-day review |\\n| Platform-Engineer | repo:admin | multi-project | dash:write | infra | full | vault:admin | Broad access required for ops teams; requires security onboarding checklist |\\n\\n*repo:admin for Level-3 is scoped to staging and infra-adjacent repos only.\\n\\nProvisioning process (first-day onboarding)\\n1) Hiring manager creates a People Ops onboarding request in Workday/HRIS and links the candidate start date.\\n2) Manager files an Access Request ticket in Jira using template: \\\"Access Request: New Hire - <NAME> - <TEAM> - <ROLE TEMPLATE>\\\". Include start date and required projects.\\n3) people-ops triages: validates manager, picks correct role template, and initiates Okta provisioning flows.\\n4) Core accounts to create: Okta account, GitHub account (SAML link), Slack, GCP IAM invite, Datadog, Confluence.\\n5) Owner (people-ops) confirms repo and project invites; manager completes the New Hire Checklist and schedules Security Onboarding session.\\n\\nExpected times:\\n- Okta and Slack: within 2 hours of ticket acknowledgement.\\n- GitHub & GCP invites: within 4 hours.\\n- All core tooling active and verified: target within 8 business hours.\\n\\nManager checklist for first 3 days\\n- Verify that the contributor can clone the repo and run the local dev script (tools/dev-setup.sh).\\n- Confirm access to Jira board and Datadog dashboards used by the team.\\n- Run through the security checklist: 2FA enforced, passwordless keys setup, vault read only.\\n- Submit permission escalation requests for protected branches if needed (see Escalation flow).\\n\\nPermission escalation flow (protected or prod access)\\n1) Engineer or manager opens a \\\"Privilege Escalation\\\" Jira ticket with justification, duration, and list of specific resources.\\n2) Security reviews and responds within 2 business days. If approved, a scoped temporary role is created (max 90 days).\\n3) Audit log entry created; approver is added as owner.\\n4) 7 days before expiry, system sends reminders to the owner and manager to extend or revert access.\\n\\nCross-team rotations and role transitions\\n- When a contributor changes teams, the new manager must:\\n  - Open a change request ticket to add new role template and remove prior team templates.\\n  - Schedule a knowledge transfer and update on-call and pager duty rosters if applicable.\\n  - Verify completed de-escalation of previous team secrets and remove access to prior projects.\\n- people-ops will run an automated script (rotation-reconcile) that compares current Okta groups to team rosters and flags mismatches weekly.\\n\\nPromotion-specific tool changes\\n- Promotion to IC-3 or above triggers a permissions review: expected changes include elevated staging permissions and write access to internal infra repos.\\n- Manager must document the promotion in the \\\"Promotion Access\\\" ticket and indicate any necessary temporary exceptions.\\n\\nDeprovisioning (offboarding)\\n1) Offboard event triggers: manager submits Offboard ticket in Jira or HRIS marks termination/leave.\\n2) Immediate actions (within 2 hours): suspend Okta session, remove Slack privileges, revoke long-lived GitHub tokens.\\n3) Secondary actions (within 24 hours): remove GCP and Datadog access, rotate any secrets where the contributor was a maintainer.\\n4) Final reconciliation (within 72 hours): people-ops confirms all access removed and produces an audit report attached to the Offboard ticket.\\n\\nEscalation playbook for stuck provisioning\\n- If new hire lacks access after 8 business hours: manager escalates to people-ops-ops channel and pings the people-ops oncall.\\n- If an access change is refused by security for unclear reasons: open a security-appeal with evidence and invite the security reviewer to a 30-minute working session.\\n\\nAudit and quarterly clean-up\\n- Quarterly automated audit runs across Okta, GitHub org, GCP IAM, and Datadog.\\n- Flags generated: stale groups (>90 days), inactive users with elevated roles, long-lived tokens.\\n- people-ops and security jointly triage and close flags within 30 days.\\n\\nTooling snippets and examples\\n- Access request JSON example (paste into Jira ticket):\\n  {\\\"candidate\\\": \\\"First Last\\\", \\\"team\\\": \\\"Platform\\\", \\\"role_template\\\": \\\"IC-Engineer-Level-2\\\", \\\"projects\\\": [\\\"project-dev-a\\\", \\\"project-infra-test\\\"], \\\"start_date\\\": \\\"2026-11-01\\\", \\\"justification\\\": \\\"Standard onboarding for backend engineer\\\"}\\n\\n- CLI to verify GitHub team membership (example):\\n  gh api repos/org/repo/teams --jq '.[] | select(.name==\\\"platform\\\") | .members_count'\\n\\nOwnership and SLAs\\n- people-ops: primary owner for provisioning and deprovisioning SLAs.\\n- Security: owner for privilege escalations and audits.\\n- Team manager: owner for role correctness and business justifications.\\n- SLA targets: provisioning complete within 8 business hours (95%), deprovisioning within 24 hours (100% for suspension).\\n\\nTemplates & attachments\\n- New Hire Access Request (Jira template): create issue type ONBOARD-ACCESS with fields: name, start_date, role_template, projects, repo_list, manager_approver.\\n- Offboard checklist (attached to offboard ticket): suspend Okta session, revoke tokens, rotate secrets, remove from oncall, archive workspace.\\n\\nCommon FAQs\\n- Q: What if the new hire needs production access on day 1?\\n  A: Production access requires an explicit Privilege Escalation ticket plus security approval. Expect 48\\u201372 hour lead time.\\n- Q: Who can request temporary elevated roles?\\n  A: Only the hire\\u2019s manager or a Director-level approver; all requests create audit trail entries.\\n\\nChange history\\n- 2026-03-15 \\u2014 initial draft (Asha Patel).\\n- 2026-07-07 \\u2014 added rotation-reconcile automation notes (reviewers: Evan Liu).\\n- 2026-10-02 \\u2014 tightened escalation SLA and clarified deprovisioning target windows (Priya Kapoor).\\n\\nRelated resources\\n- Security onboarding checklist: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/security-onboarding-checklist-2025\\n- Onboarding toolchain mapping: /confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json\\n\\nContact\\n- people-ops oncall: #people-ops-urgent (Slack).\\n- Security escalation: security-escalations@redwood.ai\\n\\nEnd of playbook\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_7754cd5d7b4d4a7ea217f1c09c28ef3c\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Contributor Toolflow and Privileges Playbook\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/contributor-toolflow-and-privileges-playbook-2026.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: company-handbook\n\n##fra repos. - manager must document the promotion in the \" promotion access \" ticket and indicate any necessary temporary exceptions. deprovisioning ( offboarding ) 1 ) offboard event triggers : manager submits offboard ticket in jira or hris marks termination / leave. 2 ) immediate actions ( within 2 hours ) : suspend okta session, remove slack privileges, revoke long - lived github tokens. 3 ) secondary actions ( within 24 hours ) : remove gcp and datadog access, rotate any secrets where the contributor was a maintainer. 4 ) final reconciliation ( within 72 hours ) : people - ops confirms all access removed and produces an audit report attached to the offboard ticket.",

{
  "title": "Contributor Toolflow and Privileges Playbook",
  "space": "company-handbook",
  "author": "Asha Patel",
  "owner_team": "people-ops",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-03-15",
  "last_updated": "2026-10-02",
  "reviewers": [
    "Evan Liu",
    "Priya Kapoor",
    "Marco Ruiz"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "onboarding",
    "access-management",
    "tooling",
    "privileges",
    "deprovisioning"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json",
    "/confluence/company-handbook/02_roles-and-career/competency-maps-and-rotation-paths-2027.json"
  ],
  "content": "Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents the standard tool access lifecycle for contributors at Redwood — from first-day provisioning through promotions, cross-team rotations, and final deprovisioning. The emphasis is on fast enablement, least-privilege by default, auditable changes, and clear manager/engineer responsibilities.

Audience: people-ops, hiring managers, engineering managers, IT, security reviewers, and new contributors.

Summary of goals:
- Ensure 95% of new hires have usable accounts and core tool access within 8 business hours of start.
- Enforce least-privilege role assignments for 90% of contributors by role templates.
- Complete deprovisioning within 24 hours for offboarded contributors (per security SLA).

Key principles
- Least privilege: grant only the roles required for the contributor’s current responsibilities.
- Role templates: use standardized permission packages (see Role → Tool mapping).
- Manager-driven exceptions: any deviation requires manager justification and a 90-day review.
- Auditability: every access change must be recorded in Okta and the access-request ticket.

Role → Tool mapping (canonical templates)
| Role | GitHub | GCP (project) | Datadog | Jira | Slack | Console/Secrets | Notes |
|------|--------|----------------|---------|------|-------|----------------|-------|
| IC-Engineer-Level-1 | repo:read | viewer | dash:read | dev-project | full | vault:read | Standard new-hire dev access (no prod) |
| IC-Engineer-Level-2 | repo:write | dev-editor | dash:read | dev-squad | full | vault:read | Can merge to non-protected branches; needs sprint leads approval for protected branches |
| IC-Engineer-Level-3 | repo:admin* | staging-editor | dash:write | squad-admin | full | vault:deploy | Elevated staging access; production access by exception and 90-day review |
| Platform-Engineer | repo:admin | multi-project | dash:write | infra | full | vault:admin | Broad access required for ops teams; requires security onboarding checklist |

*repo:admin for Level-3 is scoped to staging and infra-adjacent repos only.

Provisioning process (first-day onboarding)
1) Hiring manager creates a People Ops onboarding request in Workday/HRIS and links the candidate start date.
2) Manager files an Access Request ticket in Jira using template: "Access Request: New Hire - <NAME> - <TEAM> - <ROLE TEMPLATE>". Include start date and required projects.
3) people-ops triages: validates manager, picks correct role template, and initiates Okta provisioning flows.
4) Core accounts to create: Okta account, GitHub account (SAML link), Slack, GCP IAM invite, Datadog, Confluence.
5) Owner (people-ops) confirms repo and project invites; manager completes the New Hire Checklist and schedules Security Onboarding session.

Expected times:
- Okta and Slack: within 2 hours of ticket acknowledgement.
- GitHub & GCP invites: within 4 hours.
- All core tooling active and verified: target within 8 business hours.

Manager checklist for first 3 days
- Verify that the contributor can clone the repo and run the local dev script (tools/dev-setup.sh).
- Confirm access to Jira board and Datadog dashboards used by the team.
- Run through the security checklist: 2FA enforced, passwordless keys setup, vault read only.
- Submit permission escalation requests for protected branches if needed (see Escalation flow).

Permission escalation flow (protected or prod access)
1) Engineer or manager opens a "Privilege Escalation" Jira ticket with justification, duration, and list of specific resources.
2) Security reviews and responds within 2 business days. If approved, a scoped temporary role is created (max 90 days).
3) Audit log entry created; approver is added as owner.
4) 7 days before expiry, system sends reminders to the owner and manager to extend or revert access.

Cross-team rotations and role transitions
- When a contributor changes teams, the new manager must:
  - Open a change request ticket to add new role template and remove prior team templates.
  - Schedule a knowledge transfer and update on-call and pager duty rosters if applicable.
  - Verify completed de-escalation of previous team secrets and remove access to prior projects.
- people-ops will run an automated script (rotation-reconcile) that compares current Okta groups to team rosters and flags mismatches weekly.

Promotion-specific tool changes
- Promotion to IC-3 or above triggers a permissions review: expected changes include elevated staging permissions and write access to internal infra repos.
- Manager must document the promotion in the "Promotion Access" ticket and indicate any necessary temporary exceptions.

Deprovisioning (offboarding)
1) Offboard event triggers: manager submits Offboard ticket in Jira or HRIS marks termination/leave.
2) Immediate actions (within 2 hours): suspend Okta session, remove Slack privileges, revoke long-lived GitHub tokens.
3) Secondary actions (within 24 hours): remove GCP and Datadog access, rotate any secrets where the contributor was a maintainer.
4) Final reconciliation (within 72 hours): people-ops confirms all access removed and produces an audit report attached to the Offboard ticket.

Escalation playbook for stuck provisioning
- If new hire lacks access after 8 business hours: manager escalates to people-ops-ops channel and pings the people-ops oncall.
- If an access change is refused by security for unclear reasons: open a security-appeal with evidence and invite the security reviewer to a 30-minute working session.

Audit and quarterly clean-up
- Quarterly automated audit runs across Okta, GitHub org, GCP IAM, and Datadog.
- Flags generated: stale groups (>90 days), inactive users with elevated roles, long-lived tokens.
- people-ops and security jointly triage and close flags within 30 days.

Tooling snippets and examples
- Access request JSON example (paste into Jira ticket):
  {"candidate": "First Last", "team": "Platform", "role_template": "IC-Engineer-Level-2", "projects": ["project-dev-a", "project-infra-test"], "start_date": "2026-11-01", "justification": "Standard onboarding for backend engineer"}

- CLI to verify GitHub team membership (example):
  gh api repos/org/repo/teams --jq '.[] | select(.name=="platform") | .members_count'

Ownership and SLAs
- people-ops: primary owner for provisioning and deprovisioning SLAs.
- Security: owner for privilege escalations and audits.
- Team manager: owner for role correctness and business justifications.
- SLA targets: provisioning complete within 8 business hours (95%), deprovisioning within 24 hours (100% for suspension).

Templates & attachments
- New Hire Access Request (Jira template): create issue type ONBOARD-ACCESS with fields: name, start_date, role_template, projects, repo_list, manager_approver.
- Offboard checklist (attached to offboard ticket): suspend Okta session, revoke tokens, rotate secrets, remove from oncall, archive workspace.

Common FAQs
- Q: What if the new hire needs production access on day 1?
  A: Production access requires an explicit Privilege Escalation ticket plus security approval. Expect 48–72 hour lead time.
- Q: Who can request temporary elevated roles?
  A: Only the hire’s manager or a Director-level approver; all requests create audit trail entries.

Change history
- 2026-03-15 — initial draft (Asha Patel).
- 2026-07-07 — added rotation-reconcile automation notes (reviewers: Evan Liu).
- 2026-10-02 — tightened escalation SLA and clarified deprovisioning target windows (Priya Kapoor).

Related resources
- Security onboarding checklist: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/security-onboarding-checklist-2025
- Onboarding toolchain mapping: /confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json

Contact
- people-ops oncall: #people-ops-urgent (Slack).
- Security escalation: security-escalations@redwood.ai

End of playbook",

  "content_field_names": [
    "content"
  ],

{
  "document": {
    "id": "enterprise_b9e03890a22cfc276b5468d4",
    "path": "/code/litellm/CONTRIBUTING.md",
    "title": "litellm: CONTRIBUTING.md",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/codebase/litellm",
    "content": "# Contributing to LiteLLM\n\nThank you for your interest in contributing to LiteLLM! We welcome contributions of all kinds - from bug fixes and documentation improvements to new features and integrations.\n\n## **Checklist before submitting a PR**\n\nHere are the core requirements for any PR submitted to LiteLLM:\n\n- [ ] **Sign the Contributor License Agreement (CLA)** - [see details](#contributor-license-agreement-cla)\n- [ ] **Keep scope isolated** - Your changes should address 1 specific problem at a time\n\n#### Proxy (Backend) PRs\n\n- [ ] **Add testing** - Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement - [see details](#adding-testing)\n- [ ] **Ensure your PR passes all checks**:\n  - [ ] [Unit Tests](#running-unit-tests) - `make test-unit`\n  - [ ] [Linting / Formatting](#running-linting-and-formatting-checks) - `make lint`\n\n#### UI PRs\n\n- [ ] **Ensure the UI builds successfully** - `npm run build`\n- [ ] **Ensure all UI unit tests pass** - `npm run test`\n- [ ] **Add tests for new components or logic** - If you are adding a new component or new logic, add corresponding tests\n\n## **Contributor License Agreement (CLA)**\n\nBefore contributing code to LiteLLM, you must sign our [Contributor License Agreement (CLA)](https://cla-assistant.io/BerriAI/litellm). This is a legal requirement for all contributions to be merged into the main repository.\n\n**Important:** We strongly recommend reviewing and signing the CLA before starting work on your contribution to avoid any delays in the PR process.\n\n## Quick Start\n\n### 1. Setup Your Local Development Environment\n\n```bash\n# Fork the repository on GitHub (click the Fork button at https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm)\n# Then clone your fork locally\ngit clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/litellm.git\ncd litellm\n\n# Create a new branch for your feature (see \"Commit and Branch Conventions\" below)\ngit checkout -b feature/your-feature\n\n# Install development dependencies\nmake install-dev\n\n# Install git hooks that enforce commit + branch conventions (one-time, opt-in)\nmake install-hooks\n\n# Verify your setup works\nmake help\n```\n\nThat's it! Your local development environment is ready.\n\n## Commit and Branch Conventions\n\nCommits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) and branches follow [Conventional Branches](https://conventional-branch.github.io/). Run `make install-hooks` once per clone to enable the local git hooks that enforce these — see the [contributor docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code#commit-and-branch-conventions) for the full type list, examples, the protected-branch bypass list, and how to opt out.\n\n### 2. Development Workflow\n\nHere's the recommended workflow for making changes:\n\n```bash\n# Make your changes to the code\n# ...\n\n# Format your code (auto-fixes formatting issues)\nmake format\n\n# Run all linting checks (matches CI exactly)\nmake lint\n\n# Run unit tests to ensure nothing is broken\nmake test-unit\n\n# Commit your changes (must follow Conventional Commits — see above)\ngit add .\ngit commit -m \"feat(scope): your descriptive commit message\"\n\n# Push and create a PR (branch must follow Conventional Branches — see above)\ngit push origin feature/your-feature\n```\n\n## Adding Testing\n\n**Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement for all PRs.**\n\n### Where to Add Tests\n\nAdd your tests to the [`tests/test_litellm/` directory](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/main/tests/test_litellm).\n\n- This directory mirrors the structure of the `litellm/` directory\n- **Only add mocked tests** - no real LLM API calls in this directory\n- For integration tests with real APIs, use the appropriate test directories\n\n### File Naming Convention\n\nThe `tests/test_litellm/` directory follows the same structure as `litellm/`:\n\n- `litellm/proxy/caching_routes.py` → `tests/test_litellm/proxy/test_caching_routes.py`\n- `litellm/utils.py` → `tests/test_litellm/test_utils.py`\n\n### Example Test\n\n```python\nimport pytest\nfrom litellm import completion\n\ndef test_your_feature():\n    \"\"\"Test your feature with a descriptive docstring.\"\"\"\n    # Arrange\n    messages = [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Hello\"}]\n    \n    # Act\n    # Use mocked responses, not real API calls\n    \n    # Assert\n    assert expected_result == actual_result\n```\n\n## Running Tests and Checks\n\n### Running Unit Tests\n\nRun all unit tests (uses parallel execution for speed):\n\n```bash\nmake test-unit\n```\n\nIf you're running broader test suites, proxy tests, or anything that touches PostgreSQL-backed fixtures/plugins, install the full local test environment first:\n\n```bash\nmake install-test-deps\n```\n\nThis syncs the locked test environment used across the repo, including `psycopg` v3 plus `psycopg-binary` (used by `pytest-postgresql`), `psycopg2-binary` (used by some proxy E2E tests), and a generated Prisma client for DB-backed proxy tests, so pytest startup matches CI without manual package installs.\n\nRun specific test files:\n```bash\nuv run pytest tests/test_litellm/test_your_file.py -v\n```\n\n### Running Linting and Formatting Checks\n\nRun all linting checks (matches CI exactly):\n\n```bash\nmake lint\n```\n\nIndividual linting commands:\n```bash\nmake format-check       # Check Black formatting\nmake lint-ruff          # Run Ruff linting\nmake lint-basedpyright  # Run basedpyright type checking\nmake check-circular-imports    # Check for circular imports\nmake check-import-safety       # Check import safety\n```\n\nApply formatting (auto-fixes issues):\n```bash\nmake format\n```\n\n> **Black formatting is enforced in CI.** All PRs must pass the Black formatting check.\n>\n> - **AI coding agents** (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, etc.): `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` instruct agents to run `poetry run black .` before committing.\n> - **VS Code users**: Install the [Black Formatter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.black-formatter) and enable format-on-save:\n>   ```json\n>   {\n>     \"[python]\": {\n>       \"editor.defaultFormatter\": \"ms-python.black-formatter\",\n>       \"editor.formatOnSave\": true\n>     }\n>   }\n>   ```\n\n### CI Compatibility\n\nTo ensure your changes will pass CI, run the exact same checks locally:\n\n```bash\n# This runs the same checks as the GitHub workflows\nmake lint\nmake test-unit\n```\n\nFor exact CI compatibility (pins OpenAI version like CI):\n```bash\nmake install-dev-ci     # Installs exact CI dependencies\n```\n\n## Available Make Commands\n\nRun `make help` to see all available commands:\n\n```bash\nmake help                       # Show all available commands\nmake install-dev               # Install development dependencies\nmake install-proxy-dev         # Install proxy development dependencies\nmake install-test-deps         # Install the full local test environment\nmake format                    # Apply Black code formatting\nmake format-check              # Check Black formatting (matches CI)\nmake lint                      # Run all linting checks\nmake test-unit                 # Run unit tests\nmake test-integration          # Run integration tests\nmake test-unit-helm            # Run Helm unit tests\n```\n\n## Code Quality Standards\n\nLiteLLM follows the [Google Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html).\n\nOur automated quality checks include:\n- **Black** for consistent code formatting\n- **Ruff** for linting and code quality\n- **basedpyright** for static type checking\n- **Circular import detection**\n- **Import safety validation**\n\nAll checks must pass before your PR can be merged.\n\n## Common Issues and Solutions\n\n### 1. Linting Failures\n\nIf `make lint` fails:\n\n1. **Formatting issues**: Run `make format` to auto-fix\n2. **Ruff issues**: Check the output and fix manually\n3. **basedpyright issues**: Add proper type hints\n4. **Circular imports**: Refactor import dependencies\n5. **Import safety**: Fix any unprotected imports\n\n### 2. Test Failures\n\nIf `make test-unit` fails:\n\n1. Check if you broke existing functionality\n2. Add tests for your new code\n3. Ensure tests use mocks, not real API calls\n4. Check test file naming conventions\n\n### 3. Common Development Tips\n\n- **Use type hints**: basedpyright requires proper type annotations\n- **Write descriptive commit messages**: Help reviewers understand your changes\n- **Keep PRs focused**: One feature/fix per PR\n- **Test edge cases**: Don't just test the happy path\n- **Update documentation**: If you change APIs, update docs\n\n## Building and Running Locally\n\n### LiteLLM Proxy Server\n\nTo run the proxy server locally:\n\n```bash\n# Install proxy dependencies\nmake install-proxy-dev\n\n# Start the proxy server\nuv run litellm --config your_config.yaml\n```\n\n### Docker Development\n\nIf you want to build the Docker image yourself:\n\n```bash\n# Build using the non-root Dockerfile\ndocker build -f docker/Dockerfile.non_root -t litellm_dev .\n\n# Run with your config\ndocker run \\\n    -v $(pwd)/proxy_config.yaml:/app/config.yaml \\\n    -e LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=\"sk-1234\" \\\n    -p 4000:4000 \\\n    litellm_dev \\\n    --config /app/config.yaml --detailed_debug\n```\n\n## UI Development\n\n### 1. Setup Your Local UI Development Environment\n\n```bash\n# Clone the repo (if you haven't already)\ngit clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/litellm.git\ncd litellm\n\n# Navigate to the UI dashboard directory\ncd ui/litellm-dashboard\n\n# Install dependencies\nnpm install\n\n# Start the development server\nnpm run dev\n```\n\n### 2. Adding UI Tests\n\nIf you are adding a **new component** or **new logic**, you must add corresponding tests.\n\n### 3. Running UI Unit Tests\n\n```bash\nnpm run test\n```\n\n### 4. Building the UI\n\nEnsure the UI builds successfully before submitting your PR:\n\n```bash\nnpm run build\n```\n\n## Submitting Your PR\n\n1. **Push your branch**: `git push origin your-feature-branch`\n2. **Create a PR**: Go to GitHub and open a pull request against [`litellm_internal_staging`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/litellm_internal_staging), which is the default base branch. Do not target `main`.\n3. **Fill out the PR template**: Provide clear description of changes\n4. **Wait for review**: Maintainers will review and provide feedback\n5. **Address feedback**: Make requested changes and push updates\n6. **Merge**: Once approved, your PR will be merged!\n\n## Getting Help\n\nIf you need help:\n\n- 💬 [Join our Discord](https://discord.gg/wuPM9dRgDw)\n- 💬 [Join our Slack](https://www.litellm.ai/support)\n- 📧 Email us: ishaan@berri.ai / krrish@berri.ai\n- 🐛 [Create an issue](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/new)\n\n## What to Contribute\n\nLooking for ideas? Check out:\n\n- 🐛 [Good first issues](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/labels/good%20first%20issue)\n- 🚀 [Feature requests](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/labels/enhancement)\n- 📚 Documentation improvements\n- 🧪 Test coverage improvements\n- 🔌 New LLM provider integrations\n\nThank you for contributing to LiteLLM! 🚀 \n",

document.content:
# Contributing to LiteLLM

Thank you for your interest in contributing to LiteLLM! We welcome contributions of all kinds - from bug fixes and documentation improvements to new features and integrations.

## **Checklist before submitting a PR**

Here are the core requirements for any PR submitted to LiteLLM:

- [ ] **Sign the Contributor License Agreement (CLA)** - [see details](#contributor-license-agreement-cla)
- [ ] **Keep scope isolated** - Your changes should address 1 specific problem at a time

#### Proxy (Backend) PRs

- [ ] **Add testing** - Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement - [see details](#adding-testing)
- [ ] **Ensure your PR passes all checks**:
  - [ ] [Unit Tests](#running-unit-tests) - `make test-unit`
  - [ ] [Linting / Formatting](#running-linting-and-formatting-checks) - `make lint`

#### UI PRs

- [ ] **Ensure the UI builds successfully** - `npm run build`
- [ ] **Ensure all UI unit tests pass** - `npm run test`
- [ ] **Add tests for new components or logic** - If you are adding a new component or new logic, add corresponding tests

## **Contributor License Agreement (CLA)**

Before contributing code to LiteLLM, you must sign our [Contributor License Agreement (CLA)](https://cla-assistant.io/BerriAI/litellm). This is a legal requirement for all contributions to be merged into the main repository.

**Important:** We strongly recommend reviewing and signing the CLA before starting work on your contribution to avoid any delays in the PR process.

## Quick Start

### 1. Setup Your Local Development Environment

```bash
# Fork the repository on GitHub (click the Fork button at https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm)
# Then clone your fork locally
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/litellm.git
cd litellm

# Create a new branch for your feature (see "Commit and Branch Conventions" below)
git checkout -b feature/your-feature

# Install development dependencies
make install-dev

# Install git hooks that enforce commit + branch conventions (one-time, opt-in)
make install-hooks

# Verify your setup works
make help
```

That's it! Your local development environment is ready.

## Commit and Branch Conventions

Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) and branches follow [Conventional Branches](https://conventional-branch.github.io/). Run `make install-hooks` once per clone to enable the local git hooks that enforce these — see the [contributor docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code#commit-and-branch-conventions) for the full type list, examples, the protected-branch bypass list, and how to opt out.

### 2. Development Workflow

Here's the recommended workflow for making changes:

```bash
# Make your changes to the code
# ...

# Format your code (auto-fixes formatting issues)
make format

# Run all linting checks (matches CI exactly)
make lint

# Run unit tests to ensure nothing is broken
make test-unit

# Commit your changes (must follow Conventional Commits — see above)
git add .
git commit -m "feat(scope): your descriptive commit message"

# Push and create a PR (branch must follow Conventional Branches — see above)
git push origin feature/your-feature
```

## Adding Testing

**Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement for all PRs.**

### Where to Add Tests

Add your tests to the [`tests/test_litellm/` directory](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/main/tests/test_litellm).

- This directory mirrors the structure of the `litellm/` directory
- **Only add mocked tests** - no real LLM API calls in this directory
- For integration tests with real APIs, use the appropriate test directories

### File Naming Convention

The `tests/test_litellm/` directory follows the same structure as `litellm/`:

- `litellm/proxy/caching_routes.py` → `tests/test_litellm/proxy/test_caching_routes.py`
- `litellm/utils.py` → `tests/test_litellm/test_utils.py`

### Example Test

```python
import pytest
from litellm import completion

def test_your_feature():
    """Test your feature with a descriptive docstring."""
    # Arrange
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
    
    # Act
    # Use mocked responses, not real API calls
    
    # Assert
    assert expected_result == actual_result
```

## Running Tests and Checks

### Running Unit Tests

Run all unit tests (uses parallel execution for speed):

```bash
make test-unit
```

If you're running broader test suites, proxy tests, or anything that touches PostgreSQL-backed fixtures/plugins, install the full local test environment first:

```bash
make install-test-deps
```

This syncs the locked test environment used across the repo, including `psycopg` v3 plus `psycopg-binary` (used by `pytest-postgresql`), `psycopg2-binary` (used by some proxy E2E tests), and a generated Prisma client for DB-backed proxy tests, so pytest startup matches CI without manual package installs.

Run specific test files:
```bash
uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/test_your_file.py -v
```

### Running Linting and Formatting Checks

Run all linting checks (matches CI exactly):

```bash
make lint
```

Individual linting commands:
```bash
make format-check       # Check Black formatting
make lint-ruff          # Run Ruff linting
make lint-basedpyright  # Run basedpyright type checking
make check-circular-imports    # Check for circular imports
make check-import-safety       # Check import safety
```

Apply formatting (auto-fixes issues):
```bash
make format
```

> **Black formatting is enforced in CI.** All PRs must pass the Black formatting check.
>
> - **AI coding agents** (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, etc.): `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` instruct agents to run `poetry run black .` before committing.
> - **VS Code users**: Install the [Black Formatter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.black-formatter) and enable format-on-save:
>   ```json
>   {
>     "[python]": {
>       "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.black-formatter",
>       "editor.formatOnSave": true
>     }
>   }
>   ```

### CI Compatibility

To ensure your changes will pass CI, run the exact same checks locally:

```bash
# This runs the same checks as the GitHub workflows
make lint
make test-unit
```

For exact CI compatibility (pins OpenAI version like CI):
```bash
make install-dev-ci     # Installs exact CI dependencies
```

## Available Make Commands

Run `make help` to see all available commands:

```bash
make help                       # Show all available commands
make install-dev               # Install development dependencies
make install-proxy-dev         # Install proxy development dependencies
make install-test-deps         # Install the full local test environment
make format                    # Apply Black code formatting
make format-check              # Check Black formatting (matches CI)
make lint                      # Run all linting checks
make test-unit                 # Run unit tests
make test-integration          # Run integration tests
make test-unit-helm            # Run Helm unit tests
```

## Code Quality Standards

LiteLLM follows the [Google Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html).

Our automated quality checks include:
- **Black** for consistent code formatting
- **Ruff** for linting and code quality
- **basedpyright** for static type checking
- **Circular import detection**
- **Import safety validation**

All checks must pass before your PR can be merged.

## Common Issues and Solutions

### 1. Linting Failures

If `make lint` fails:

1. **Formatting issues**: Run `make format` to auto-fix
2. **Ruff issues**: Check the output and fix manually
3. **basedpyright issues**: Add proper type hints
4. **Circular imports**: Refactor import dependencies
5. **Import safety**: Fix any unprotected imports

### 2. Test Failures

If `make test-unit` fails:

1. Check if you broke existing functionality
2. Add tests for your new code
3. Ensure tests use mocks, not real API calls
4. Check test file naming conventions

### 3. Common Development Tips

- **Use type hints**: basedpyright requires proper type annotations
- **Write descriptive commit messages**: Help reviewers understand your changes
- **Keep PRs focused**: One feature/fix per PR
- **Test edge cases**: Don't just test the happy path
- **Update documentation**: If you change APIs, update docs

## Building and Running Locally

### LiteLLM Proxy Server

To run the proxy server locally:

```bash
# Install proxy dependencies
make install-proxy-dev

# Start the proxy server
uv run litellm --config your_config.yaml
```

### Docker Development

If you want to build the Docker image yourself:

```bash
# Build using the non-root Dockerfile
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.non_root -t litellm_dev .

# Run with your config
docker run \
    -v $(pwd)/proxy_config.yaml:/app/config.yaml \
    -e LITELLM_MASTER_KEY="sk-1234" \
    -p 4000:4000 \
    litellm_dev \
    --config /app/config.yaml --detailed_debug
```

## UI Development

### 1. Setup Your Local UI Development Environment

```bash
# Clone the repo (if you haven't already)
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/litellm.git
cd litellm

# Navigate to the UI dashboard directory
cd ui/litellm-dashboard

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start the development server
npm run dev
```

### 2. Adding UI Tests

If you are adding a **new component** or **new logic**, you must add corresponding tests.

### 3. Running UI Unit Tests

```bash
npm run test
```

### 4. Building the UI

Ensure the UI builds successfully before submitting your PR:

```bash
npm run build
```

## Submitting Your PR

1. **Push your branch**: `git push origin your-feature-branch`
2. **Create a PR**: Go to GitHub and open a pull request against [`litellm_internal_staging`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/litellm_internal_staging), which is the default base branch. Do not target `main`.
3. **Fill out the PR template**: Provide clear description of changes
4. **Wait for review**: Maintainers will review and provide feedback
5. **Address feedback**: Make requested changes and push updates
6. **Merge**: Once approved, your PR will be merged!

## Getting Help

If you need help:

- 💬 [Join our Discord](https://discord.gg/wuPM9dRgDw)
- 💬 [Join our Slack](https://www.litellm.ai/support)
- 📧 Email us: ishaan@berri.ai / krrish@berri.ai
- 🐛 [Create an issue](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/new)

## What to Contribute

Looking for ideas? Check out:

- 🐛 [Good first issues](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/labels/good%20first%20issue)
- 🚀 [Feature requests](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/labels/enhancement)
- 📚 Documentation improvements
- 🧪 Test coverage improvements
- 🔌 New LLM provider integrations

Thank you for contributing to LiteLLM! 🚀

  "document": {
    "id": "enterprise_ffc0390514a198a0f0bb9f75",
    "path": "/code/litellm/tests/e2e/CONTRIBUTING.md",
    "title": "litellm: tests/e2e/CONTRIBUTING.md",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/codebase/litellm",
    "content": "# Contributors Guide\n\nThis directory holds the live end-to-end suites that prove product correctness against a real running proxy and real provider APIs. The goal of this guide is simple: when you ship a feature, you add e2e coverage that walks that feature the way production does, across every route and edge case it touches, so a later change that breaks it fails here first\n\nRead this before adding a test and i recommend reading through CLAUDE.md\n\nWhen contributing to this directory, please first discuss the change you wish to make via issue or pull request. We require screenshots and proof of your tests working on a live proxy. \n\n\n## Setup\n\nThe suites run against a live proxy, so bring one up first by running the litellm proxy locally. Point it at a config that prewires the example models the suites use (`gpt-5.5`, `claude-haiku-4-5`, `gemini-2.5-flash`, `openai-text-embedding-3-small`) with keys from your `.env`, and enables prompt storage, a redis cache, and the fast budget rescheduler the quota suites rely on. If your test needs another model, a pricing override, or a guardrail declared up front, add it to that config and read it back in the test rather than hardcoding values\n\n## Running the tests locally\n\n1. Create a `.env` file in this directory with the provider keys the example models use, plus the master key and the Postgres/Redis coordinates your config reads back:\n\n   ```bash\n   LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=\"sk-1234\"\n   DATABASE_URL=\"postgresql://llmproxy:dbpassword9090@localhost:5432/litellm\"\n   REDIS_HOST=\"localhost\"\n   REDIS_PORT=\"6379\"\n   OPENAI_API_KEY=\"sk-...\"\n   ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=\"sk-...\"\n   GEMINI_API_KEY=\"...\"\n   ```\n\n2. Bring up a Postgres and a Redis for the proxy to use. The repo-root `docker-compose.yml` already defines a Postgres on `5432`; a `docker run -p 6379:6379 redis:7` covers Redis. Point `DATABASE_URL` / `REDIS_HOST` / `REDIS_PORT` at whatever you run\n\n3. Start the litellm proxy locally against your config and confirm it is live:\n\n   ```bash\n   set -a && source .env && set +a\n   litellm --config <your-e2e-config>.yml --port 4000\n   curl -fs http://localhost:4000/health/liveliness\n   ```\n\n4. Run a suite against it; the harness reads `LITELLM_PROXY_URL` (default `http://localhost:4000`):\n\n   ```bash\n   uv run pytest tests/e2e/llm_translation/ -v\n   ```\n\n   The browser tests in the `management/` suite drive the dashboard the proxy serves at `/ui` through playwright, an optional dependency behind `importorskip` (the suite's API tests run without it). It lives in the `e2e-dev` dependency group; install it along with its browser:\n\n   ```bash\n   uv sync --inexact --group e2e-dev\n   uv run playwright install chromium\n   ```\n\n   They also need a proxy whose bundled UI contains the change under test, so run the proxy from your branch (an editable install serves the UI your checkout builds)\n\nSome suites need extra services the bare proxy does not start. The `logging/` OTEL trace-completeness tests read spans back from a jaeger query API at `http://localhost:16686` (override with `E2E_OTEL_QUERY_URL`); run a `jaegertracing/all-in-one` and point `PHOENIX_COLLECTOR_HTTP_ENDPOINT` at its OTLP ingest. The `mcp/` suite needs the deterministic upstream MCP server in `mcp_tests/mcp_e2e_upstream_server.py` reachable by the proxy\n\nTests marked `@pytest.mark.e2e` hard-fail when no proxy answers `/health/liveliness`, so a run that goes red with `No live proxy` at setup means the proxy isn't up; they never skip for a missing proxy, so an absent proxy can't be mistaken for a pass\n\n## What a complete test looks like\n\nA feature test is complete only when it walks the feature end to end, in this order\n\n1. CREATE the resource (key / team / budget / ...) and immediately queue its deletion\n2. CONFIGURE the feature's setting on it (assign the budget, turn on compression, set the limit)\n3. ACT; drive real traffic through the gateway exactly like prod does (right model, real auth headers, enough calls to actually trigger the behavior)\n4. SETTLE; poll the DB / spend logs until the write lands. Writes are eventually consistent (spend flushes on proxy_batch_write_at, ~60s), so poll to a deadline. Never sleep once\n5. ASSERT the recorded state the feature promises (spend > budget, cost reduced, tag attributed, ...)\n6. ASSERT the enforced behavior the gateway returns (429 budget_exceeded, block, refusal, ...)\n7. TEARDOWN; every resource you created is deleted\n\n### The one rule that makes it complete\n\nIt must assert BOTH sides: the recorded state (step 5) AND the enforced behavior (step 6)\n\nA test that only checks \"the call went through\", or only checks spend without checking the 429, is not complete; it is checking plumbing, not the product promise\n\n### Example: budget enforcement\n\n```\ncreate a key                     -> (1)\nassign a budget                  -> (2)\nsend a bunch of calls            -> (3)\npoll for db spend                -> (4)\nassert spend > budget            -> (5)\nassert status_code == 429        -> (6)  (\"budget_exceeded\")\nkey auto-deleted on teardown     -> (7)\n```\n\n### The skeleton every test fills in\n\n```\nsetup     ->  create the resource + queue cleanup\nconfigure ->  apply the feature's knob\nact       ->  send real calls like production\nsettle    ->  poll the DB until the write lands\nassert    ->  recorded state is correct   (the feature happened)\nassert    ->  gateway enforced it         (the product promise held)\nteardown  ->  delete everything you created\n```\n\nIf a step is missing, the test is not done. That is the whole pattern\n\n## Style: lay the pattern down in a class\n\nKeep the cases for one feature inside a class so the file reads as a spec for how that feature behaves in production. The class name says what is under test; each method is one behavior. Think of it as documenting the contract, with the rough intent being\n\n```python\n# pseudo-code to convey intent\nclass TestPromptCompression:\n    def test_prompt_compression_add_to_virtual_key(self):\n        new_key = self.resources.create_key(user_id, compression=True)  # turn the feature on\n        resources._defer(new_key)  # queue key deletion\n\n    def test_prompt_compression_accumulate_spend(self, key_id, user_id):\n        for _ in range(10):\n            response = self.resources.proxy.post(\"gemini-2.5-flash\", key_id, user_id)\n        compressed_value = ...\n        assert response.cost == compressed_value  # the cost was actually reduced\n```\n\nThat snippet only conveys intent. What you actually write uses the real harness: the `client` fixture for your suite, the `scoped_key` fixture for an auto-deleted key, typed pydantic bodies from `models.py`, and `unwrap(...)` on the tagged-union result. `tests/e2e/llm_translation/test_custom_pricing_e2e.py` is the reference to copy from; it creates a scoped key, drives a real gemini call, polls `/spend/logs` to a deadline for the cost-breakdown row, then asserts the input and output costs match the configured custom rates and that a sibling deployment kept its own price. Read it before writing yours\n\n## Use the shared transport; never touch requests directly\n\nEvery HTTP call goes through the shared transport, never through `requests.*` in a test. `e2e_http.py` is the only module permitted to call `requests.*`, and that is enforced in CI by `tests/code_coverage_tests/check_e2e_no_raw_requests.py`. A test that imports requests will fail the check\n\nThe shape is layered so tests stay declarative\n\n`transport.py` exposes a `Transport` Protocol with `post`, `get`, `delete`, `send`, `stream`, `probe`, plus `bearer(key)` and the `master` header. `HttpTransport` fulfils it, and `SplitTransport` routes each call by path to the data plane or the control plane so a split control-plane/data-plane deployment works without any change in the test\n\n`proxy_client.py` holds `ProxyClient`, a frozen dataclass that wraps a `Transport` and adds the operations tests reuse: `generate_key` / `delete_key` / `key_info`, `model_info`, the LLM calls `chat` / `chat_stream` / `embed` / `ocr`, the spend read-back `spend_logs`, and the poll helpers `poll_logs_for_key` / `poll_logs_for_request_id` that loop to `poll_timeout` instead of sleeping once. It is exposed as the session-scoped `proxy` fixture (see tests/e2e/conftest.py), which each suite's `client` fixture depends on and injects. Add a new route as a method here so other suites get it for free\n\nEach suite provides its own `client` fixture (see `llm_translation/passthrough_client.py`), a frozen dataclass that holds the shared `ProxyClient` (as `.proxy`) and adds suite-specific routes. Cleanup runs through that same `ProxyClient`, so whatever keys or customers your test creates get torn down by the `resources` fixture\n\nRequest and response bodies are typed pydantic models in `models.py`; only the fields a test reads are modelled, and nothing passes raw dicts. Outcomes come back as a `Result[R]` tagged union (`Success`, `NetworkError`, `UnauthorizedError`, `RateLimitedError`, `ValidationError`, `UnknownApiError`). Handle them with `match`, or call `unwrap(...)` when a non-success should fail the test. The harness hard-fails and never skips: a test marked `e2e` fails when no proxy answers its liveness probe, and once a request reaches the proxy any wrong behavior is likewise a hard failure, so a missing proxy turns the run red instead of being mistaken for a pass\n\nMark live tests with `@pytest.mark.e2e` (on the class or the module). Pure coverage of the harness itself carries no marker and runs regardless. Use `scoped_key` for a fresh all-models key that auto-deletes, `resources` when you need to create and tear down more than a key, and `unique_marker()` from `e2e_config` to keep prompts, tags, and customer ids from colliding across concurrent runs and the shared response cache\n\n## Pre-commit steps\n\nBefore you push\n\n1. Run `make lint-e2e-basedpyright` (or `make pre-commit` with your changes staged); the harness is fully typed and the gate allows zero basedpyright errors, enforced in CI on any PR touching `tests/e2e/**/*.py`\n\n2. Add the models your test needs to the config your local proxy loads\n\n3. Start the litellm proxy locally and run your suite against it:\n\n   ```bash\n   litellm --config <your-e2e-config>.yml --port 4000\n   uv run pytest tests/e2e/<your_suite>/ -v\n   ```\n\n4. Capture screenshots of the test run and attach them to the PR as proof\n\n5. If a test fails because it surfaced a real issue in the product, flag that explicitly in the PR rather than reworking the test until it passes\n",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: litellm: tests/e2e/CONTRIBUTING.md\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/codebase/litellm\nPath: /code/litellm/tests/e2e/CONTRIBUTING.md\nConnector: codebase\nWorkspace: litellm\n\n1. create the resource ( key / team / budget /... ) and immediately queue its deletion 2. configure the feature ' s setting on it ( assign the budget, turn on compression, set the limit ) 3. act ; drive real traffic through the gateway exactly like prod does ( right model, real auth headers, enough calls to actually trigger the behavior ) 4. settle ; poll the db / spend logs until the write lands. writes are eventually consistent ( spend flushes on proxy _ batch _ write _ at, ~ 60s ), so poll to a deadline. never sleep once 5. assert the recorded state the feature promises ( spend > budget, cost reduced, tag attributed,... ) 6. assert the enforced behavior the gateway returns ( 429 budget _ exceeded, block, refusal,... ) 7. teardown ; every resource",

document.title: litellm: tests/e2e/CONTRIBUTING.md
document.content:
# Contributors Guide

This directory holds the live end-to-end suites that prove product correctness against a real running proxy and real provider APIs. The goal of this guide is simple: when you ship a feature, you add e2e coverage that walks that feature the way production does, across every route and edge case it touches, so a later change that breaks it fails here first

Read this before adding a test and i recommend reading through CLAUDE.md

When contributing to this directory, please first discuss the change you wish to make via issue or pull request. We require screenshots and proof of your tests working on a live proxy. 


## Setup

The suites run against a live proxy, so bring one up first by running the litellm proxy locally. Point it at a config that prewires the example models the suites use (`gpt-5.5`, `claude-haiku-4-5`, `gemini-2.5-flash`, `openai-text-embedding-3-small`) with keys from your `.env`, and enables prompt storage, a redis cache, and the fast budget rescheduler the quota suites rely on. If your test needs another model, a pricing override, or a guardrail declared up front, add it to that config and read it back in the test rather than hardcoding values

## Running the tests locally

1. Create a `.env` file in this directory with the provider keys the example models use, plus the master key and the Postgres/Redis coordinates your config reads back:

   ```bash
   LITELLM_MASTER_KEY="sk-1234"
   DATABASE_URL="postgresql://llmproxy:dbpassword9090@localhost:5432/litellm"
   REDIS_HOST="localhost"
   REDIS_PORT="6379"
   OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
   ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-..."
   GEMINI_API_KEY="..."
   ```

2. Bring up a Postgres and a Redis for the proxy to use. The repo-root `docker-compose.yml` already defines a Postgres on `5432`; a `docker run -p 6379:6379 redis:7` covers Redis. Point `DATABASE_URL` / `REDIS_HOST` / `REDIS_PORT` at whatever you run

3. Start the litellm proxy locally against your config and confirm it is live:

   ```bash
   set -a && source .env && set +a
   litellm --config <your-e2e-config>.yml --port 4000
   curl -fs http://localhost:4000/health/liveliness
   ```

4. Run a suite against it; the harness reads `LITELLM_PROXY_URL` (default `http://localhost:4000`):

   ```bash
   uv run pytest tests/e2e/llm_translation/ -v
   ```

   The browser tests in the `management/` suite drive the dashboard the proxy serves at `/ui` through playwright, an optional dependency behind `importorskip` (the suite's API tests run without it). It lives in the `e2e-dev` dependency group; install it along with its browser:

   ```bash
   uv sync --inexact --group e2e-dev
   uv run playwright install chromium
   ```

   They also need a proxy whose bundled UI contains the change under test, so run the proxy from your branch (an editable install serves the UI your checkout builds)

Some suites need extra services the bare proxy does not start. The `logging/` OTEL trace-completeness tests read spans back from a jaeger query API at `http://localhost:16686` (override with `E2E_OTEL_QUERY_URL`); run a `jaegertracing/all-in-one` and point `PHOENIX_COLLECTOR_HTTP_ENDPOINT` at its OTLP ingest. The `mcp/` suite needs the deterministic upstream MCP server in `mcp_tests/mcp_e2e_upstream_server.py` reachable by the proxy

Tests marked `@pytest.mark.e2e` hard-fail when no proxy answers `/health/liveliness`, so a run that goes red with `No live proxy` at setup means the proxy isn't up; they never skip for a missing proxy, so an absent proxy can't be mistaken for a pass

## What a complete test looks like

A feature test is complete only when it walks the feature end to end, in this order

1. CREATE the resource (key / team / budget / ...) and immediately queue its deletion
2. CONFIGURE the feature's setting on it (assign the budget, turn on compression, set the limit)
3. ACT; drive real traffic through the gateway exactly like prod does (right model, real auth headers, enough calls to actually trigger the behavior)
4. SETTLE; poll the DB / spend logs until the write lands. Writes are eventually consistent (spend flushes on proxy_batch_write_at, ~60s), so poll to a deadline. Never sleep once
5. ASSERT the recorded state the feature promises (spend > budget, cost reduced, tag attributed, ...)
6. ASSERT the enforced behavior the gateway returns (429 budget_exceeded, block, refusal, ...)
7. TEARDOWN; every resource you created is deleted

### The one rule that makes it complete

It must assert BOTH sides: the recorded state (step 5) AND the enforced behavior (step 6)

A test that only checks "the call went through", or only checks spend without checking the 429, is not complete; it is checking plumbing, not the product promise

### Example: budget enforcement

```
create a key                     -> (1)
assign a budget                  -> (2)
send a bunch of calls            -> (3)
poll for db spend                -> (4)
assert spend > budget            -> (5)
assert status_code == 429        -> (6)  ("budget_exceeded")
key auto-deleted on teardown     -> (7)
```

### The skeleton every test fills in

```
setup     ->  create the resource + queue cleanup
configure ->  apply the feature's knob
act       ->  send real calls like production
settle    ->  poll the DB until the write lands
assert    ->  recorded state is correct   (the feature happened)
assert    ->  gateway enforced it         (the product promise held)
teardown  ->  delete everything you created
```

If a step is missing, the test is not done. That is the whole pattern

## Style: lay the pattern down in a class

Keep the cases for one feature inside a class so the file reads as a spec for how that feature behaves in production. The class name says what is under test; each method is one behavior. Think of it as documenting the contract, with the rough intent being

```python
# pseudo-code to convey intent
class TestPromptCompression:
    def test_prompt_compression_add_to_virtual_key(self):
        new_key = self.resources.create_key(user_id, compression=True)  # turn the feature on
        resources._defer(new_key)  # queue key deletion

    def test_prompt_compression_accumulate_spend(self, key_id, user_id):
        for _ in range(10):
            response = self.resources.proxy.post("gemini-2.5-flash", key_id, user_id)
        compressed_value = ...
        assert response.cost == compressed_value  # the cost was actually reduced
```

That snippet only conveys intent. What you actually write uses the real harness: the `client` fixture for your suite, the `scoped_key` fixture for an auto-deleted key, typed pydantic bodies from `models.py`, and `unwrap(...)` on the tagged-union result. `tests/e2e/llm_translation/test_custom_pricing_e2e.py` is the reference to copy from; it creates a scoped key, drives a real gemini call, polls `/spend/logs` to a deadline for the cost-breakdown row, then asserts the input and output costs match the configured custom rates and that a sibling deployment kept its own price. Read it before writing yours

## Use the shared transport; never touch requests directly

Every HTTP call goes through the shared transport, never through `requests.*` in a test. `e2e_http.py` is the only module permitted to call `requests.*`, and that is enforced in CI by `tests/code_coverage_tests/check_e2e_no_raw_requests.py`. A test that imports requests will fail the check

The shape is layered so tests stay declarative

`transport.py` exposes a `Transport` Protocol with `post`, `get`, `delete`, `send`, `stream`, `probe`, plus `bearer(key)` and the `master` header. `HttpTransport` fulfils it, and `SplitTransport` routes each call by path to the data plane or the control plane so a split control-plane/data-plane deployment works without any change in the test

`proxy_client.py` holds `ProxyClient`, a frozen dataclass that wraps a `Transport` and adds the operations tests reuse: `generate_key` / `delete_key` / `key_info`, `model_info`, the LLM calls `chat` / `chat_stream` / `embed` / `ocr`, the spend read-back `spend_logs`, and the poll helpers `poll_logs_for_key` / `poll_logs_for_request_id` that loop to `poll_timeout` instead of sleeping once. It is exposed as the session-scoped `proxy` fixture (see tests/e2e/conftest.py), which each suite's `client` fixture depends on and injects. Add a new route as a method here so other suites get it for free

Each suite provides its own `client` fixture (see `llm_translation/passthrough_client.py`), a frozen dataclass that holds the shared `ProxyClient` (as `.proxy`) and adds suite-specific routes. Cleanup runs through that same `ProxyClient`, so whatever keys or customers your test creates get torn down by the `resources` fixture

Request and response bodies are typed pydantic models in `models.py`; only the fields a test reads are modelled, and nothing passes raw dicts. Outcomes come back as a `Result[R]` tagged union (`Success`, `NetworkError`, `UnauthorizedError`, `RateLimitedError`, `ValidationError`, `UnknownApiError`). Handle them with `match`, or call `unwrap(...)` when a non-success should fail the test. The harness hard-fails and never skips: a test marked `e2e` fails when no proxy answers its liveness probe, and once a request reaches the proxy any wrong behavior is likewise a hard failure, so a missing proxy turns the run red instead of being mistaken for a pass

Mark live tests with `@pytest.mark.e2e` (on the class or the module). Pure coverage of the harness itself carries no marker and runs regardless. Use `scoped_key` for a fresh all-models key that auto-deletes, `resources` when you need to create and tear down more than a key, and `unique_marker()` from `e2e_config` to keep prompts, tags, and customer ids from colliding across concurrent runs and the shared response cache

## Pre-commit steps

Before you push

1. Run `make lint-e2e-basedpyright` (or `make pre-commit` with your changes staged); the harness is fully typed and the gate allows zero basedpyright errors, enforced in CI on any PR touching `tests/e2e/**/*.py`

2. Add the models your test needs to the config your local proxy loads

3. Start the litellm proxy locally and run your suite against it:

   ```bash
   litellm --config <your-e2e-config>.yml --port 4000
   uv run pytest tests/e2e/<your_suite>/ -v
   ```

4. Capture screenshots of the test run and attach them to the PR as proof

5. If a test fails because it surfaced a real issue in the product, flag that explicitly in the PR rather than reworking the test until it passes

Changes that were not discussed in an issue may be rejected. Once we've discussed your changes and you've got your code ready, make sure that tests are passing and open your pull request. A good first step is to search for open [issues](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/issues). Issues are labeled, and some good issues to start with are labeled: [good first issue](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22). ## Project Overview We recommend checking out DeepWiki to familiarize yourself with the project: [![Ask DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/badge.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/langfuse/langfuse) ### Technologies we use - Application (this repository) - NextJS 14, pages router - NextAuth.js / Auth.js - tRPC: Frontend APIs - Prisma ORM - Zod v4 - Tailwind CSS - shadcn/ui tailwind components (using Radix and tanstack) - Fern: generate OpenAPI spec and Pydantic models - JS SDK ([langfuse/langfuse-js](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse-js)) - openapi-typescript to generated types based on OpenAPI spec - Python SDK ([langfuse/langfuse-python](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse-python)) - Pydantic for input validation, models generated by fern ### Architecture Overview See this [diagram](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting#architecture) for an overview of the architecture. ### Network Overview ```mermaid flowchart TB User["UI, API, SDKs"] subgraph vpc["VPC"] Web["Web Server
(langfuse/langfuse)"] Worker["Async Worker

For instance, `trace_id` in the `observation` table is not defined as a foreign key to the `trace` table to allow unordered ingestion of these objects, but it is still a foreign key in the application code. Full database schema: [packages/shared/prisma/schema.prisma](packages/shared/prisma/schema.prisma) ## Repository Structure We built a monorepo using [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/motivation) and [turbo](https://turbo.build/repo/docs) to manage the dependencies and build process. The monorepo contains the following packages: - `web`: is the main application package providing Frontend and Backend APIs for Langfuse. - `worker`: contains an application for asynchronous processing of tasks. - `packages`: - `shared`: contains shared code between the above packages. - `config-eslint`: contains eslint configurations which are shared between the above packages. - `config-typescript`: contains typescript configurations which are shared between the above packages. - `ee`: contains all enterprise features. See [EE README](ee/README.md) for more details. ## Development Setup Requirements - Node.js 24 as specified in the [.nvmrc](.nvmrc) - Pnpm v.11.10.0 - Docker to run the database locally - Clickhouse client **Note:** You can also simply run Langfuse in a **GitHub Codespace** via the provided devcontainer. To do this, click on the green "Code" button in the top right corner of the repository and select "Open with Codespaces". ### Codex Cloud Setup You can also attach this repository to an OpenAI Codex cloud environment. The cloud environment itself is configured in the Codex UI, while the repo-owned bootstrap is versioned in: - `scripts/codex/setup.sh` - `scripts/codex/maintenance.sh` Recommended Codex UI configuration: 1. Create a new cloud environment for this repository in the Codex UI. 2. Choose a base environment with Node.js 24 support. 3. Set the setup script to: ```bash bash scripts/codex/setup.sh ``` 4. Set the maintenance script to: ```bash bash scripts/codex/maintenance.sh ``` 5. Keep internet access disabled by default, or only allow the minimum domains needed for your task. 6. Add secrets and environment variables in the Codex UI instead of committing them to the repository. Notes: - This Codex setup is intended for repository tasks such as code changes, linting, typechecking, and targeted tests. - It does **not** start the full Langfuse stack. Local development still uses Docker and `pnpm run dx` / `pnpm run dev`. - Running the full application inside Codex requires external services for PostgreSQL, Redis, ClickHouse, and object storage, plus matching environment variables in the Codex UI. ### Shared Agent Setup This repository keeps the shared agent setup in source control so developers using different tools can work against the same instructions, bootstrap, and MCP server catalog. - Canonical shared docs: - `.agents/AGENTS.md` - Root discovery symlinks: - `AGENTS.md` - `CLAUDE.md` - Shared agent setup overview: `.agents/README.md` - Shared skills: `.agents/skills/` - Shared tool/bootstrap/MCP config: `.agents/config.json` - Tool-specific MCP configs generated locally from that catalog and not committed: - `.mcp.json` - `.cursor/mcp.json` - `.vscode/mcp.json` - `.codex/config.toml` - Tool-specific runtime shims generated locally from the shared config and not committed: - `.claude/settings.json` - `.codex/environments/environment.toml` - `.cursor/environment.json` - Tool-specific skill projections generated locally and not committed: - `.claude/skills/*` - Shared bootstrap for agent environments: `bash scripts/codex/setup.sh` When you change the shared MCP setup: 1. Edit `.agents/config.json` 2. Run `pnpm run agents:sync` 3. Run `pnpm run agents:check` 4. Do not commit the generated MCP config files or runtime shims **Steps** 1. Install development dependencies: - [golang-migrate](https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/tree/master/cmd/migrate#migrate-cli) as CLI - [clickhouse binary](https://clickhouse.com/docs/install) on macOS with brew: `curl https://clickhouse.com/ | sh` 2. Fork the repository and clone it locally ```bash git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git cd langfuse ``` 3. Install dependencies and set up pre-commit hooks ```bash pnpm install pnpm run prepare # Sets up Husky pre-commit hooks for code formatting ``` The pre-commit hook runs formatting and lint checks. To skip only the lint check for a commit, set `LANGFUSE_PRE_COMMIT_SKIP_LINT`, for example: ```bash LANGFUSE_PRE_COMMIT_SKIP_LINT=1 git commit -m "your commit message" ``` CI still runs the required checks for pull requests. 4. Create an env file ```bash cp .env.dev.example .env ``` 5. Run the entire infrastructure in dev mode. **Note**: if you have an existing database, this command wipes it. Also, this will fail on the very first run. Please run it again. ```bash pnpm run dx # first run only (resets db, docker containers, etc...) pnpm run dev # any subsequent runs ``` You will be asked whether you want to reset Postgres and ClickHouse. Confirm both with 'Y' and press enter. 6. Open the web app in your browser to start using Langfuse: - [Sign up page, http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) - [Demo project, http://localhost:3000/project/7a88fb47-b4e2-43b8-a06c-a5ce950dc53a](http://localhost:3000/project/7a88fb47-b4e2-43b8-a06c-a5ce950dc53a) 7. Log in as a test user: - Username: `demo@langfuse.com` - Password: `password` To get comprehensive example data, you can use the `seed` command: ```sh pnpm run db:seed:examples ``` ## Monorepo quickstart - Available packages and their dependencies Packages are included in the monorepo according to the `pnpm-workspace.yaml` file. Each package maintains its own dependencies defined in the `package.json`. Internal dependencies can be added as well by adding them to the package dependencies: `"@langfuse/shared": "workspace:*"`. - Executing commands You can run commands in all packages at once. For example, to install all dependencies in all packages, you can execute: ```bash pnpm install pnpm run dev pnpm --filter=web run dev # execute command only in one package pnpm tc # fast typecheck all packages pnpm build:check # Full Next.js build to alternate dir (can run parallel with dev server) ``` In the root `package.json`, you can find scripts which are executed with turbo e.g. `turbo run dev`. These scripts are executed with the help of Turbo. Turbo executes the commands in all packages taking care of the correct order of execution. Task definitions can be found in the `turbo.config.js` file. - Run migrations To run migrations, you can execute the following command. ```bash pnpm run db:migrate -- --name ``` > [!NOTE] > If you frequently switch branches, use `pnpm run dx` instead of `pnpm run dev`. This command will install dependencies, reset the database (wipe and apply all migrations), and run the database seeder with example data before starting the development server. > [!NOTE] > If you find yourself stuck and want to clean the repo, execute `pnpm run nuke`. It will remove all node_modules and build files. ## System behavior ### Ingestion API `(/public/api/ingestion)` - the ingestion API takes different event types (creation and updates of traces, generations, spans, events) - The API loops through each event and: - validates the event - stores the event raw in the events table - calculates tokens for `generations` - matches models from the `models` table to model for `generations` events - upserts the event in the `traces` or `observations` table - returns a `207` HTTP status code with a list of errors if any event failed to be ingested ## Commit messages On the main branch, we adhere to the best practices of [conventional commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). All pull requests and branches are squash-merged to maintain a clean and readable history. This approach ensures the addition of a conventional commit message when merging contributions. ## Running Unit Tests All tests run in the CI and must pass before merging. All tests run against a running langfuse instance and **write/delete real data from the database**. ### Test Database Setup Per default, the tests use the local development database. Therefore, wiping your data in the process. For proper test isolation, create a `.env.test` file in the root directory: ```bash cp .env.test.example .env.test ``` Then, a different PostgreSQL and Redis are used for the tests. The `.env.test` file only overrides the set values and falls back on `.env` for all undefined values. - **PostgreSQL**: Uses separate `langfuse_test` database for isolation - **ClickHouse**: Uses shared `default` database for now - **Redis**: Uses database 1 instead of 0 for isolation (Redis data is not cleaned between tests) Tests automatically create the PostgreSQL test database if it doesn't exist and clean up data between runs. ### Tests in the `web` package (public API) We're using Vitest in the `web` package. There are two types of unit tests: - `test` (server tests) - `test-client` To run a specific test by name within a file, run: ```sh cd web # or use `pnpm --filter web test ...` from the repository root pnpm test prompts.v2.servertest -t "should handle special characters in prompt names" ``` To run all tests: ```sh pnpm run test ``` Run interactively in watch mode (not recommended!) ```sh pnpm run test:watch ``` ### Tests in the `worker` package For the `worker` package, we're also using Vitest to run unit tests. ```sh pnpm --filter worker run test FILE_YOU_WANT_TO_TEST.ts -t "test name" ``` ## CI/CD We use GitHub Actions for CI/CD, the configuration is in [`.github/workflows/pipeline.yml`](.github/workflows/pipeline.yml) CI on `main` and `pull_request` - Check Linting - E2E test of API using Vitest - E2E tests of UI using Playwright CD on `main` - Publish Docker image to GitHub Packages if CI passes. Done on every push to `main` branch. Only released versions are tagged with `latest`. ## Staging environment We run a staging environment at [https://staging.langfuse.com](https://staging.langfuse.com) that is automatically deployed on every push to `main` branch. The same environment is also used for preview deployments of pull requests. Limitations: - SSO is not available as dynamic domains are not supported by most SSO providers. - When making changes to the database, migrations to the staging database need to be applied manually by a maintainer. If you want to interactively test database changes in the staging environment, please reach out. You can use the staging environment end-to-end with the Langfuse integrations or SDKs (host: `https://staging.langfuse.com`). However, please note that the staging environment is not intended for production use and may be reset at any time. ## Production environment We run two separate release/deployment processes: 1. **Langfuse Cloud deployment (frequent):** - Every commit on the `production` branch triggers an ECS deployment to Langfuse Cloud. - To deploy current `main` to Langfuse Cloud, promote `main` to `production` via [`promote-main-to-production.yml`](.github/workflows/promote-main-to-production.yml) (instead of force pushing from a local machine). 2. **Open-source release (less frequent):** - The open-source Docker release process is handled via [`release.yml`](.github/workflows/release.yml) for self-hosted production users. You can trigger the Langfuse Cloud promotion in either way: 1. Preferred local command: ```bash pnpm run release:cloud ``` This wraps the GitHub CLI trigger and performs preflight checks (main branch/sync checks and migration diff checks against `production`) before dispatching the workflow. 2. GitHub UI: open **Actions** -> **Promote Main to Production** -> **Run workflow**, then set `confirm=promote`. ## Theming At Langfuse, we utilize CSS variables to manage our theme settings across the platform. Our approach leverages separate CSS variables for backgrounds (--background) and foregrounds (--foreground), fully adhering to the [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming) color conventions. The background suffix can be omitted if the variable is used for the background color of the component. We recommend using HSL values for these colors to enhance consistency and customization. There is no need to manually handle dark mode styling with "dark:" prefixes, as next-themes automatically manages the theme switching. Given the following CSS variables: ``` --primary: 222.2 47.4% 11.2%; // e.g. background-color --primary-foreground: 210 40% 98%; // e.g. text-color ``` The background color of the following component will be `hsl(var(--primary))` and the foreground color will be `hsl(var(--primary-foreground))`. ```
